claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy has an initial dual-phase microstructure.
Intermediate-temperature aging at approximately 500–600 °C can nucleate fine, coherent precipitates at eutectic interfaces in as-cast AlCoCrFeNi.
Nucleation of fine, coherent interfacial precipitates can retain or transiently improve toughness.
Extending aging beyond an optimal time window causes the precipitates to coarsen.
Coarsening of the precipitates causes embrittlement.
A temperature-and-time window exists in which fine precipitates can nucleate without significant coarsening.
The proposed aging conditions mirror embrittlement and recovery treatments used in similar thermal or thermomechanical regimes.
Fine precipitates at phase boundaries impede crack initiation and propagation.
Coarsened precipitates act as stress-concentration sites.
Stress concentrations associated with coarsened precipitates promote embrittlement.
Samples aged for an optimal duration should retain or slightly improve toughness relative to the as-cast baseline.
Samples aged for excessively long durations should have lower toughness than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply to AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloys subjected to intermediate-temperature aging.
The behavior may differ outside the specified temperature range or in alloys with substantially different compositions or dominant phases.
The optimal aging time and temperature may vary with composition and processing details.
Aging at a fixed temperature such as 550 °C over multiple durations, followed by toughness and microscopy measurements, can test the proposed time-dependent behavior.

The hypothesis is falsified if nominally optimal aging fails to retain toughness relative to the as-cast control, or if prolonged aging and precipitate coarsening do not correlate with reduced toughness.
